analysis: 'Eliza Russell Aged 7 Years 1834' -- a dated, named, house-and-verse sampler, and a genuinely good one. The photograph shows an alphabet band over a moralising verse, a middle register of flowering urns, birds and stylised trees, a large three-bay brick house with a pink roof flanked by conical topiary and a fence, and a strawberry-vine border on all four sides. The colour survival is exceptional: the pinks and greens are still strong rather than faded to biscuit, which is what separates a $600 sampler from a $1,500 one. It sits in a period figured mahogany veneer frame. And 'aged 7 years' is remarkably young for work of this complexity, which the sampler market rewards. Estimated $600-800, which is the low end of what this should make.
problems: At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band, so there is little headroom if two collectors want it. The house form -- steep gables with finials, three bays, brick -- reads English or Welsh rather than American, and American samplers command a substantial premium over British ones, so do not price this as American work. Check the ground linen for weakness and the reverse for old repairs and a backing, and confirm the frame's glazing is not sitting directly on the silk. There is a small dark stain at the lower left of the frame.
patience: Moderate. Dated samplers run through New England sales regularly, but ones with a house, a verse, a named seven-year-old and colour this well preserved are the top decile.

analysis: A four-colour two-panel Jacquard coverlet with the corner blocks woven 'SAMUEL MUNDWILER / SENECA COUNTY OHIO' and a date. Four colours -- red, indigo, gold and natural -- is the good grade; most surviving coverlets are two-colour blue-and-white. The signed and dated corner block is the American coverlet market's equivalent of a maker's mark: it names the weaver, the county and the year, which is documentary evidence of a kind almost nothing else in this sale carries. The colours in the photograph are strong and unfaded. Estimated $300-500, which is at or below the market.
problems: The edges are the problem and the photograph shows it: fringe loss along the bottom and both lower corners, with fraying and a small loss at the left edge. That is normal wear for a used bedcover and it is where the money comes off. Check the centre seam where the two panels join -- it splits -- and hold it to light for moth damage in the indigo, which is where wool moths go first. Ohio rather than New England, so no regional premium for a Maine buyer.
patience: Moderate. Signed Jacquard coverlets run regularly; four-colour ones with legible blocks are the smaller share.

analysis: An 1836 Jacquard coverlet by John Brosey of Manheim, Pennsylvania, $600-800. Dated to the year with a named weaver and a named town -- the same documentary quality as 2134 and two years older. Manheim is in Lancaster County, the heartland of Pennsylvania German weaving, and Brosey is a documented weaver.
problems: At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band, where 2134 is comfortably inside it. Same condition checklist: fringe, centre seam, moth. Pennsylvania coverlets are also the most abundant of all American coverlets, so the maker's name does less lifting here than it would from a scarcer region. If both this and 2134 come up, 2134 is the better value.
patience: Moderate to high. Pennsylvania Jacquard coverlets are the deepest supply in the category.

analysis: An early needlework sampler by R.M. Holmes, $2,000-3,000. The estimate is four times that of the Eliza Russell sampler at 2131, which means the house thinks this is either much earlier, American, or both -- and those are exactly the two things that multiply sampler prices. Above the band at $2,640-3,960 all-in.
problems: Above budget. 'Early' with no date is a strange omission on a sampler, since samplers almost always carry their own date -- if this one does not, the estimate rests on style rather than evidence, and that is a weak foundation at $2,000-3,000. Only two photographs on the highest-estimated textile in the sale.

analysis: A small framed 39-star US silk flag, $300-500. The 39-star flag is one of the great American flag curiosities: no 39-star flag was ever official. Manufacturers anticipated that the Dakota Territory would enter the Union as a single state in 1889, made flags accordingly, and were caught out when it split into North and South Dakota and the count jumped to 42. That makes a genuine 39-star flag a dated artefact of a specific few months in 1889, comfortably antique, and a good story to own. Inside the band.
problems: Because 39-star flags are collectable, they are reproduced -- and printed-on-silk parade flags are the easiest thing in the world to reprint. The tells are the silk itself (period silk is fragile, slubby and has usually shattered somewhere), the printing register, and the hem or staff sleeve. Silk parade flags of this age shatter along the folds and the damage is usually hidden by the mount. Framed, so the reverse and the edges cannot be seen.
patience: Moderate. Star-count flags run in Americana sales; the 39-star is the one people look for.

analysis: A large Claire Murray hooked rug, 7'6" x 8'6", bird and flowers, 'Cottage Squares', $1,000-1,500 -- one of two Claire Murray lots (see 2153). Claire Murray is a Nantucket designer whose hooked-rug patterns were sold as kits and as finished pieces from the 1980s onward; the designs are pretty and the New England association is real, but this is contemporary decorative work, not antique hooked rug.
problems: The estimate is the trap. Claire Murray rugs resell for a fraction of their original retail -- a large one in good condition makes $200-600 at auction, not $1,000-1,500. This is a category where the original price tag has been mistaken for a value. Kit-hooked rugs also vary enormously in execution depending on who worked them, and that is not addressed. Post-1926 by six decades and no criteria fit.
patience: Very high. Claire Murray rugs are abundant in New England sales.

analysis: A large Claire Murray hooked rug, 8' x 9', bird and flowers, 'Cottage Corners', $1,000-1,500. Companion to 2149 and the same conclusion.
problems: Same as 2149, and the two compete directly in the same session.

analysis: A handmade tatted bed coverlet, 8' x 7'6", $300-400. Tatting a coverlet of this size is thousands of hours of hand work with a shuttle, and the result is a genuine piece of domestic craft rather than anything manufactured. Tatted and crocheted coverlets were made from the later 19th century into the mid-20th.
problems: No date, so it may or may not clear 1926. The market for white needlework coverlets has collapsed almost completely -- they are laborious to make, impossible to launder safely and nobody has a bed for them. Expect discolouration and broken threads. The estimate is above the market by a factor of two or three; buy only well below it, and buy for the craft rather than the value.

analysis: A pair of Chinese embroidered silk skirt panels, catalogued Qing dynasty, $300-500. Catalogued to the dynasty, so a pre-1912 claim the house can be held to, and Qing embroidered silk is genuinely fine work -- Peking knot, satin stitch and couched gold on figured ground. Skirt panels are the affordable entry to Chinese textiles because they are fragments of a garment rather than the garment.
problems: Qing embroidery is heavily reproduced and the modern Suzhou workshops are excellent. Silk of this age also shatters: hold panels to the light and look for splits along the fold lines and losses in the ground where the metallic threads have cut it. Panels are frequently made up from several garments. Any panel with what appears to be kingfisher-feather work would raise a separate wildlife-material question.
patience: High. Qing textile fragments run steadily in Asian sales.

analysis: A Chinese embroidered silk lady's short robe, late Qing, $500-700 -- one of two identically described lots (see 2478). A complete garment rather than a panel, catalogued to the late Qing, so genuinely antique. Women's informal short robes with embroidered sleeve bands and borders are appealing wearable-scale objects and display well.
problems: At $660-924 all-in it is at the top of the band. Silk garments of this age are almost always shattered somewhere in the ground silk, and linings are usually replaced. Two identical lots in the same session compete with each other. Reproduction Qing-style robes are made in quantity for costume and decorative use.
patience: High -- there is a second one in this very sale.

analysis: A Chinese embroidered silk lady's short robe, late Qing, $500-700 -- word for word the same as 2475, three lots later. See that entry, and bid whichever is cheaper.
problems: Same as 2475, and directly competing with it.

analysis: A Chinese blue-ground summer dragon robe, late Qing, $2,000-3,000. Dragon robes are court dress and the summer gauze versions are the scarcer and more delicate form. Catalogued to the late Qing, so genuinely antique, and the best Chinese textile in the sale. Three to four times the band at $2,640-3,960 all-in.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin. Dragon robes are extensively reproduced and also frequently 'improved' -- borders and cuffs added, roundels reapplied -- and the rank details (number of claws, roundel placement, the sleeve bands) need reading by someone who knows the system. Summer gauze is exceptionally fragile. Note that some period court robes incorporate kingfisher feather or peacock-thread elements with their own restrictions.
patience: Moderate. Dragon robes appear in most Asian sales; good summer ones less often.

analysis: Eight Peruvian textiles and two Coptic, framed, $1,500-2,000. The Coptic fragments are the interesting part: Egyptian Coptic tapestry weave dates from roughly the 4th to the 9th century, which would make them by far the oldest objects in the sale -- older than everything else by a millennium. Above the band at $1,980-2,640 all-in.
problems: Above budget. And the provenance question is serious rather than technical: pre-Columbian Andean textiles and Coptic fragments both come under cultural-property restrictions -- Peru has a US bilateral agreement restricting import of pre-Columbian material, and Egyptian antiquities require documented export. Buying framed fragments with no stated provenance is a real exposure. Also, both categories are convincingly faked, and framing hides the reverse where the evidence is.

analysis: A framed Turkish textile, $500-700 -- presumably an Ottoman embroidery or a metal-thread panel. Ottoman needlework of the 18th and 19th centuries is genuine and attractive, and framing a fragment is the usual way these survive. Same consignment as the Iznik group (2431-2438), which suggests a single Ottoman source.
problems: No date, no type, no technique named -- 'Turkish textile' could be a 19th-century embroidered towel end, a metal-thread bohca, or a 20th-century decorative panel. At $660-924 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band for something entirely undescribed. Framing hides the reverse, which on embroidery is where the technique and age are read.

analysis: Wendy Jones Cartwright, embroidery artist, $400-600 -- one of two identical lots (see 1340). A living or recent embroidery artist with no established auction record; the standing principle about unindexed names applies directly.
problems: No title, no date, no dimensions, no medium beyond 'embroidery'. Contemporary textile art has essentially no secondary market. Two identical lots competing. Estimate is a gallery number.

analysis: Wendy Jones Cartwright, embroidery artist, $400-600 -- identical to 1338. See that entry.
problems: Same as 1338.

analysis: An Anatolian kilim, 5'6" x 12'6", $600-800 -- a long flatweave, likely two panels joined, which is how large Anatolian kilims were traditionally woven. Kilims are the one part of the rug market with a design-driven audience that has held up better than knotted-pile Persians, because they read as graphic art rather than as floor covering.
problems: No date. The Anatolian kilim market runs from 19th-century village pieces with natural dyes to 1970s commercial production, and the difference is entirely in the dyes and the wool -- neither of which resolves in a catalogue line. Check the join, the selvedges and whether the reds are cochineal and madder or synthetic. Flatweaves also wear through and are often heavily rewoven. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band.
patience: Very high. This is one of thirty rugs and carpets in a single Day 2 consignment.

analysis: A Karabagh prayer rug, 11'2" x 4', $500-700. Karabagh weaving from the southern Caucasus is a genuine tradition and Caucasian rugs are the part of the oriental rug market with the most serious collector following. But the dimensions given are those of a long runner, not a prayer rug -- prayer rugs are small, roughly 3' x 5', and a 4' x 11' piece is a kellei or a runner. The description is internally inconsistent.
problems: The title and the measurements disagree, which means one of them is wrong and neither can be relied on. No date. Caucasian rugs are also the most reproduced, with modern Azeri and Afghan weaves copying old Karabagh designs. Ends and sides on a long rug of this age are usually rewoven.

analysis: A Shirvan kilim, $500-700 -- dimensions given as 5'5" x 9", which is obviously a typographical error for 9'. Shirvan is an eastern Caucasian weaving region with a real collector base.
problems: The stated dimensions are wrong on their face, which is a small thing but indicative -- this is a large consignment catalogued quickly. No date. Same dye-and-wool question as every other rug here.

analysis: A Daghestan prayer rug, 3'3" x 4'6", $500-700 -- and this one's dimensions actually are prayer-rug dimensions, unlike 1378. Daghestan prayer rugs with lattice fields are among the most recognisable and most collected Caucasian weavings, and the small size makes it a wall piece rather than furniture.
problems: No date, and 19th-century Daghestans are a different market from 20th-century ones. Small Caucasian prayer rugs are also the most copied format. Check the ends -- prayer rugs get worn at the bottom where feet go. At $660-924 all-in it is at the top of the band.

analysis: A pair of Indo-Mahal small carpets, 5'6" x 8'6", $1,200-1,500. 'Indo-' is the trade prefix for Indian workshop production copying a Persian design -- in this case Mahal -- and it means modern commercial weaving, not antique. A matched pair is itself a production signal; antique carpets do not come in pairs.
problems: Above the band at $1,584-1,980 all-in for modern commercial carpets. The Indo-Persian market has fallen further than the antique one. No date, and none needed: the name says it.

analysis: A large Persian rug, 12'2" x 9'4", $1,000-2,000 -- the opening lot of the Day 2 rug consignment, roughly thirty carpets running from 2172 to 2271. The whole group needs one framing judgement: the oriental rug market has fallen further than almost any other decorative category since 2010, and room-size decorative Persians that made $3,000-5,000 twenty years ago now make $600-1,500. Estimates across this consignment are broadly at or above the current market, and almost every lot is above the buyer's band.
problems: Above budget. 'Large Persian rug' with no region, no date and no knot count is the least specific description in the group -- when a cataloguer can name Heriz, Kashan and Sarouk on neighbouring lots and writes only 'Persian' here, that is a piece they could not place. Room-size rugs are also a shipping and siting commitment.
patience: Very high. Thirty carpets in this sale alone.

analysis: A Heriz rug, 11'2" x 8'2", $1,000-2,000. Heriz is the most commercially successful of all Persian carpet types in America and there are three of them in this consignment (2175, 2181, 2226). Above the band.
problems: Above budget. No date, and Heriz has been woven continuously for a century and a half -- a 1900 Heriz and a 1980 Heriz look similar in a photograph and differ several-fold in price. Three Heriz lots competing in one session.

analysis: A Heriz rug, 10'8" x 9'4", $800-1,200. Second of three Heriz lots. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget, undated, competing with 2175 and 2226.

analysis: A Heriz carpet, 10'3" x 13'3", $1,500-2,500 -- the largest and highest-estimated of the three Heriz lots. Two to three times the band.
problems: Above budget. Undated. Thirteen feet is a room-size commitment.

analysis: A Kashan carpet, 10'2" x 14'6", $1,500-2,000. Kashan is a fine city weave and the large carpets are technically impressive. Two to three times the band.
problems: Above budget. Undated. Kashan production spans the whole 20th century and modern Indo-Kashans copy it. Two Kashan lots in the consignment (see 2189).

analysis: A Kashan rug, 4'1" x 6'8", $1,000-1,500 -- the smaller of the two Kashans and the more liveable size. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Undated.

analysis: A Kazak long rug, dimensions given as 4" x 9'6" (obviously 4' x 9'6"), $1,000-1,500. Kazak is a Caucasian type and Caucasian weaving is the collector end of this consignment. Above the band.
problems: Above budget. Undated -- and on a Kazak the date is everything, since 19th-century Kazaks are a serious market and 20th-century ones are not. Another dimension typo in the catalogue.

analysis: A 'classic Ardebil carpet', 8'1" x 10'4", $1,000-1,500. 'Ardebil' invokes the most famous Persian carpet in the world -- the 1539 Ardabil in the V&A -- which is what the word 'classic' is doing here. This is a 20th-century carpet in the Ardabil medallion design. Above the band.
problems: Above budget. The name is doing promotional work. Undated.

analysis: A Chinese carpet, 12'4" x 15'2", $1,000-1,500 -- one of three Chinese carpet lots (2197, 2249, 2251). Fifteen feet is a ballroom. Above the band.
problems: Above budget. Undated. Chinese carpets of the 20th century are the softest part of an already soft market -- the thick-pile Peking and Tientsin carpets in particular are close to unsaleable at any size. Enormous.

analysis: A Chinese carpet, 16'3" x 13'3", $3,000-4,000 -- the highest-estimated rug in the sale and one of the largest. Four to five times the band.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin. Undated. Sixteen feet of Chinese carpet is a difficult object to place and an expensive one to move.

analysis: A Chinese Deco rug, 9'1" x 11'7", $2,000-3,000. The Nichols and Fette-Li Art Deco Chinese carpets of the 1920s and 30s are the one genuinely collected corner of the Chinese carpet market -- they have a design following rather than a rug following, which is why they hold value while the rest of the category falls. This one straddles the antique line. Above the band at $2,640-3,960 all-in.
problems: Above budget. No maker and no date given, and on Chinese Deco rugs the Nichols signature is most of the value. Deco rugs are also reproduced in India today in the same palettes.
patience: Moderate. Chinese Deco is the one part of this consignment with a real audience.

analysis: A Bakhtiari carpet, 6'9" x 9'10", $1,000-1,200. Bakhtiari garden-panel carpets are sturdy village weaving with a distinctive compartmented design. Above the band at $1,320-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Undated. Bakhtiari carpets are among the most abundant Persian village types in the American market.

analysis: A Sarouk rug, 11'5" x 7'11", $1,000-1,500. American Sarouks -- the rose-ground floral carpets sold by the tens of thousands in the 1920s-40s -- are the single most oversupplied Persian type in the United States. Above the band.
problems: Above budget. Undated. Many American-market Sarouks were chemically stripped and painted at the port to suit American taste, and the paint wears off unevenly; check the pile at the base against the tips.
patience: Very high. Sarouks are in every estate sale in New England.

analysis: A Persian tile-pattern rug, 11'6" x 8'10", $1,000-1,500. A repeating panel design, undated, region unnamed. Above the band.
problems: Above budget. No region, no date. 'Tile pattern' is a description of the design, not an attribution.

analysis: A Pakistan Bokhara carpet, 8'10" x 12'10", $800-1,200. Pakistani Bokharas -- the repeating-gul carpets woven in Lahore and Karachi from the 1950s onward -- are commercial production, not tribal weaving, and the market for them is close to nil.
problems: Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in for a modern commercial carpet. The estimate is many times what these make; large Pakistani Bokharas regularly fail to sell at $200. This is the clearest overestimate in the rug consignment.

analysis: A Caucasian rug, 3'8" x 6'1", $800-1,200. A liveable size and Caucasian weaving is the collector end of the category, but no region is named -- Kazak, Shirvan, Kuba, Karabagh and Daghestan all price differently -- and no date is given. Above the band.
problems: Above budget at $1,056-1,584 all-in. 'Caucasian' with no region and no date is the least you can say about a Caucasian rug.

analysis: A small Caucasian rug, 5'7" x 3'6", $400-600 -- the cheapest Caucasian lot in the consignment and a genuinely useful size. Inside the band at $528-792 all-in, which most of these are not.
problems: No region, no date, same as 2215. But at this estimate the risk is proportionate: if it turns out to be a 20th-century Azeri copy you have paid a fair price for a decorative rug, and if it is an older village piece you have done well. Check the back for depressed knots and the ends for reweaving.

analysis: A Kurdistan Herati-design carpet, 4'4" x 6'7", $800-1,200. Kurdish village weaving is robust and honest, and the Herati is the most common Persian repeating field pattern. Above the band.
problems: Above budget at $1,056-1,584 all-in. Undated.

analysis: A Serab runner, 10'4" x 3', $1,000-1,500. Serab (Serapi's neighbour) camel-ground runners are attractive and the format is genuinely useful in a hallway. Above the band.
problems: Above budget. Undated. Runners take the most foot traffic of any rug format and wear at the ends first.

analysis: A Persian Lavar Kerman pictorial rug, 3'5" x 5'1", $600-800. Lavar Kerman is the fine grade of Kerman weaving, and pictorial rugs -- portraits, hunting scenes, garden scenes -- are the interesting corner of the category because they are pictures rather than patterns. Small, wall-hangable, and the most individual rug in the consignment.
problems: At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band. No date, and no subject named, which for a pictorial rug is a strange omission -- the subject is the whole point. Kerman pictorials are also reproduced. Silk-highlighted examples fade badly.
patience: Moderate to high. Pictorial Kermans are the less common format within a common type.

analysis: A wool pictorial carpet, 9'9" x 8', $800-1,200. No origin, no date, no subject. Above the band.
problems: Above budget. The least-described lot in the rug consignment: neither where it was woven, nor when, nor what it depicts.

analysis: A Persian carpet, 11'5" x 8', $700-900. No region, no date. Above the band at $924-1,188 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Generic description.

analysis: A Hamadan rug, 12'8" x 9', $800-1,000. Hamadan is the largest weaving region in Iran by volume and its carpets are the most abundant Persians in America. Above the band.
problems: Above budget at $1,056-1,320 all-in. Undated. Hamadan production is single-wefted and coarse; these are working carpets, not collectors' ones.

analysis: A Karadja runner, 2'3" x 13', $600-800. Karadja runners with their triple-medallion repeats are one of the more recognisable northwest Persian formats. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band.
problems: Undated. Thirteen feet of runner needs thirteen feet of hallway. Ends and edges take the wear.

analysis: An 'oriental rug', 8' x 10', $400-600 -- the least described and one of the cheapest lots in the consignment, and inside the band at $528-792 all-in. When a cataloguer working through thirty rugs writes only 'oriental rug', they have stopped trying; that occasionally means an opportunity and more often means a tired carpet.
problems: No origin, no date, no design. Nothing to assess without seeing it. If it is worn or has holes, the estimate is optimistic; if it is a sound decorative carpet, it is roughly right.

analysis: A 'floral rug', 8'1" x 5'5", $500-700. Another generic title, a useful size, and inside the band at $660-924 all-in only just.
problems: No origin, no date, no design beyond 'floral'. Same assessment problem as 2258.

analysis: An abrashed Persian rug, 6'6" x 4'7", $400-600. 'Abrash' is the horizontal colour banding produced when a weaver moves between dye lots -- it is a mark of hand-dyed wool and small-batch village weaving, and collectors read it as a positive rather than a fault. Naming it in the title is the most informative thing said about any rug in this consignment. Inside the band.
problems: Abrash is also imitated in modern production because the market likes it, so its presence is suggestive rather than conclusive. No date, no region. Good size, fair price, unverifiable claim.

analysis: A Chinese wool deer rug, 2'7" x 5'1", $300-500. A small pictorial Chinese rug with a deer -- more of a picture than a floor covering at this size. The cheapest rug in the consignment and inside the band.
problems: Undated. Chinese pictorial rugs of the mid-20th century are decorative and have almost no collector market. Small size limits it to a wall or a hall.

analysis: An early 20th-century Tekke Bokhara rug, 6'9" x 9'10", $600-800 -- and it is the only rug in the entire thirty-lot consignment that carries a date. Tekke Turkmen weaving with the repeating gul field is a genuine tribal tradition and 'early 20th century' puts it on or just inside the 1926 line. The one lot here where the cataloguer committed to anything.
problems: 'Early 20th century' straddles the antique line, hence border rather than antique. Tekke designs are the most copied of all Turkmen weaving -- Pakistani and Afghan 'Bokharas' use the same gul in synthetic dyes. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band. Check for the deep madder-red ground of a real Tekke against the flatter synthetic red of a copy.

analysis: An Indo-Persian two-piece rug set, $300-500. 'Indo-Persian' is the trade term for Indian workshop production of Persian designs, and a matched two-piece set is a production signal. Modern commercial weaving.
problems: The estimate is above the market -- modern Indo-Persian rugs are worth very little on resale. No date, and none needed.

analysis: Two Tibetan wool carpets, $600-800. Tibetan and Nepali carpet weaving for export is a large modern industry; genuine antique Tibetan rugs are a specialist collecting field and look quite different from the commercial ones.
problems: No date, no size, no design. At $792-1,056 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band for what are most likely modern Nepali-woven carpets.
